newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - P&U hit by market jitters over 97 EPSI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - P&U hit by market jitters over 97 EPSI.

text.p: Market jitters over Swedish/U.S. drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn re-emerged on Thursday as the company foreshadowed weaker-than-expected earnings per share in 1997.

Confidence in P&U was boosted initially when the company posted a report for the first nine months of 1996 in line with a profit warning over negative currency effects three weeks ago. Shares rose 11 crowns to 251 crowns.
But P&U knocked the market for six when it announced at an analysts' telephone conference call later in the day that 1997 EPS was likely to fall below market forecasts of $2.35.
Shares reversed and tumbled, trading as much as 17.5 crowns lower but closing 13.5 lower at 229.5, its lowest close in nearly a year.
"It's a matter of credibility," analyst Stephen Putnam from Keinwort Benson told Reuters. "Three weeks ago we were told one thing and now the company's changed its story.
"This was like another profit warning."
P&U spokesman Jan Isoz said the company's chief finance director Bob Salisbury told analysts the EPS consensus forecast on the market for 1997 was too high.
"The average forecast is around $2.35 and he said that it could be around 10 cents too high," Isoz told Reuters.
This was expected to trigger another round of profit revisions similar to when the recently merged P&U released a surprise profit warning three weeks ago for the third quarter.

P&U unnerved investors when it said the weaker yen, stronger Swedish crown and Italian lira could drag EPS down to about 44 cents in the third quarter. Analysts expected 55 cents. Shares plummeted from 275.50 crowns to 238 crowns.
When P&U posted its nine month results on Thursday, it reported third quarter EPS of 44 cents a share, the same as a year ago, and a 12 percent drop in earnings to $204 million.
P&U's net sales rose two percent to $1.7 billion but currency effects wiped two percentage points off sales growth.
"I think the result at first was met with relief that EPS was flat and the company was on track with its merger targets," said analyst John Reeve from Paribas.
"But I think there's a growing awareness of how much (currency) hedging gains contributed to profits in 1995. People are getting a better feeling about currency contributions.
"Currency is going to be a dominant issue in 1997."
Analysts, however, were fairly confident in other areas of P&U, which was formed through a $6.9 billion merger of Sweden's Pharmacia and Upjohn from the U.S. in August 1995.

"Sales growth in some of the newly launched products was better than expected (in the third quarter)," said a British analyst, pinpointing cancer drug Camptosar, erective dysfunction product Caverjet and glaucoma drug Xalatan.
Salisbury told Reuters in a telephone interview that he expected "fairly nice growth in the fourth quarter" after a "temporary setback" in the third quarter due to currency rates.
But he said: "We expect a very nice improvement from the lower base."
Salisbury said P&U's forecast of $500 million of annual cost savings from the merger by 1998 was on track with some $425 million of this expected to be in place next year.
"Cost savings are coming through at about the same rate as we expected and analysts expected," Salisbury said.
He said these savings would help to drive the targeted improvement in operating profit margins to 25 percent of sales in 1998 from 18 percent in 1995.
"So far we have been shown nothing at all to suggest P&U won't meet these goals," one analyst said.
